title: Understanding and Mitigating Cross-Session Attacks via Persistent Artifacts in Agent Skill Composition

object.carrier: Persistent task artifacts produced during skill execution — files, configurations, database records and cached data (e.g., handoff notes with handoff_guidance fields, SQLite/JSON/XLSX artifacts, Markdown status notes) — that are retained across sessions and reused by other skills; conversation history is reset between sessions

safety_property.statement: User authorization scope, confidentiality, and integrity must not be violated by malicious influence carried through persistent artifacts written by attacker-controlled upstream skills and consumed by downstream skills in later sessions: no unauthorized disclosure, no data use beyond authorized scope, no unauthorized operations, and no false content/statuses/software changes in deliverables; the property fails when the downstream agent treats artifact content as additional user authorization or trusted factual evidence, and it is judged per run on execution evidence rather than self-report
safety_property.operationalized_as: ASR (case-specific target security consequence occurs) and ACSR (consequence realized through the intended cross-session skill-artifact chain), both confirmed by an independent Attack Judge over all 270 adversarial cases per configuration; TSR measures legitimate task completion separately

capabilities: Modifies multiple third-party skill packages before deployment, including their instructions (SKILL.md), supporting code, and bundled resources

Upstream controlled skill induces the agent to write attack-related content into persistent artifacts during a legitimate task; downstream controlled skill guides the agent to use that content in a later session
Knows the functionality and intended use scenarios of the controlled skills
Attack operates within the agent's existing file and tool permissions
assumptions: Sessions can access retained persistent artifacts but do not inherit prior conversation history
The attacker cannot observe execution results or adapt payloads during execution
The attacker cannot directly modify files between sessions, modify user tasks, trusted project policies, the underlying model, the agent scaffold, or control session boundaries
Technical ability to access data or perform an operation does not imply user authorization; neither skill instructions nor generated content can independently expand authorization
not_covered: Direct artifact tampering by the attacker between sessions
Runtime-adaptive payloads or attacker observation of execution
Attacks on the SkillRelayGuard runtime, provenance store, or the offline judges themselves
Insider or model-itself adversaries; the user is not the adversary
Repeated-run variance within a single configuration (no repeated trials)

intervention.name: SkillRelayGuard
intervention.description: A runtime defense decoupled from the task-execution agent with two enforced intervention points. (1) Skill-artifact attribution: at the end of an upstream session, an independent LLM combines the user task, skill content read, tool-call records, and workspace snapshot diffs to build provenance associations, each requiring a cited skill requirement, a matching tool record, and a corresponding artifact change; validated records (path, content hash, evidence) are stored outside the agent-writable workspace. (2) A post-tool hook restores provenance context (originating task, associated skills, evidence) plus an explicit usage boundary when a downstream agent reads an artifact, and before any operation executes through an instrumented interface an independent reviewer (GPT-5.4) checks authorization scope, data-use appropriateness, and factual support against original materials, returning reasons, evidence, and revision advice. Review is mandatory but advisory: the task-execution agent retains the final decision to revise, abandon, or confirm the request.

results.claim: On SkillRelayBench (270 adversarial cross-session cases), attacks succeeded broadly across seven model configurations on three agent frameworks: ASR ranged from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack-chain success from 35.6% to 61.1%.
results.setting: 7 model configurations (GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini-3.6-Flash, Gemini-3.7-Flash, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6) on Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Claude Code; attacker controls upstream+downstream third-party skill packages; 270 adversarial cases per configuration
results.quote: Our evaluation of seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code reveals attack success rates (ASR) ranging from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates (ACSR) ranging from 35.6% to 61.1%.

denominator.n_total: 270 adversarial cases per configuration; 1,890 runs total across seven configurations
denominator.how_counted: Each configuration is evaluated on all 270 adversarial cases in SkillRelayBench, yielding 1,890 experimental runs. (5.1)

results.claim: Pooling all 1,890 runs, the unguarded agents had an overall ASR of 64.7%, ACSR of 50.2%, and TSR of 76.3%, showing cross-session composition attacks propagate through artifact handoff even after conversation-history reset.
results.setting: Seven model configurations x 270 SkillRelayBench adversarial cases (1,890 runs), Docker-isolated non-interactive execution

denominator.n_valid: 1,223 attack successes; 948 attack-chain successes; 1,442 task successes
denominator.how_counted: Each configuration is evaluated on all 270 adversarial cases in SkillRelayBench, yielding 1,890 experimental runs. (5.1)

results.claim: In more than half of all runs (53.0%), agents completed the user's legitimate task while also achieving the attacker's objective, so task completion alone is an inadequate safety indicator.
results.setting: All 1,890 runs of seven model configurations on SkillRelayBench
results.quote: Across all 1,890 runs, 1,001 (53.0%) achieve both the user’s task and the attack objective.

denominator.n_valid: 1,001 runs judged successful for both task and attack
denominator.how_counted: Across all 1,890 runs, 1,001 (53.0%) achieve both the user’s task and the attack objective. (5.2)

results.claim: Across three agent configurations, SkillRelayGuard reduced overall ASR from 69.5% to 10.9% and ACSR from 54.8% to 10.0% (reductions of 58.6 and 44.8 pp) against attacker-controlled upstream/downstream skill packages.
results.setting: Codex CLI (GPT-5.3-Codex), Gemini CLI (Gemini-3.6-Flash), Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6); each on the same 270 adversarial SkillRelayBench cases, unguarded vs guarded
results.quote: Across the three configurations, the unguarded baseline has an overall ASR of 69.5% and ACSR of 54.8%. With SkillRelayGuard, they decrease to 10.9% and 10.0%, corresponding to reductions of 58.6 and 44.8 percentage points (pp), respectively.

denominator.n_total: 270 adversarial cases per configuration; three configurations per condition (per-config rates each over 270 cases)
denominator.n_valid: 563 attack successes unguarded vs 88 guarded; 444 vs 81 attack-chain successes (Table 6 Overall rows)
denominator.how_counted: All rates count successes confirmed by the corresponding Judge over all 270 cases per configuration. (7.1)

results.claim: Enabling SkillRelayGuard increased rather than decreased legitimate task completion: overall TSR rose from 79.6% to 87.5% (a gain of 7.9 pp) on the same adversarial cases.
results.setting: Codex CLI (GPT-5.3-Codex), Gemini CLI (Gemini-3.6-Flash), Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6); 270 adversarial cases per configuration, unguarded vs guarded
results.quote: Overall TSR rises from 79.6% to 87.5%, a gain of 7.9 percentage points.

denominator.n_total: 270 adversarial cases per configuration; three configurations per condition
denominator.n_valid: 645 task successes unguarded vs 709 guarded (Table 6 Overall rows)

results.claim: In the ablation (Codex CLI, GPT-5.3-Codex), pre-execution advisory review alone cut ASR/ACSR to 25.9%/24.8%, and adding read-time provenance context restoration (full SkillRelayGuard) further reduced them to 17.4%/17.0%, while context restoration alone was largely ineffective (ASR 73.3% vs 77.4% Vanilla).
results.comparison: Review only 25.9%/24.8% -> full 17.4%/17.0% (improvements of 8.5 and 7.8 pp)
results.setting: Codex CLI with GPT-5.3-Codex on the same 270 adversarial cases; four configurations: Vanilla, Context only, Review only, full SkillRelayGuard
results.quote: Review only reduces ASR and ACSR to 25.9% and 24.8%, providing substantially larger defense gains. The full SkillRelayGuard further reduces these rates to 17.4% and 17.0%, improvements of 8.5 and 7.8 percentage points over Review only.

denominator.how_counted: Using Codex CLI with GPT-5.3-Codex, we compare four configurations on the same 270 adversarial cases. (7.4)

results.claim: Among skill-package injection surfaces, malicious supporting code was the most effective overall, with ASR/ACSR of 70.2%/59.0%, exceeding injections into instructions (60.8%/44.4%) and bundled resources (63.2%/47.0%).
results.setting: Overall row pooling the seven model configurations on SkillRelayBench; attacks injected into upstream skill instructions, supporting code, or bundled resources
results.quote: Supporting code has the highest overall ASR and ACSR, at 70.2% and 59.0%, exceeding instructions at 60.8% and 44.4% and resources at 63.2% and 47.0%.

denominator.n_total: 90 cases per injection surface per configuration (270 = 30 scenarios x 3 patterns x 3 surfaces); Overall pools seven configurations
denominator.how_counted: Rates computed over all scheduled runs in the reported group (4.4); Table 4 Overall row pools the seven configurations

results.claim: Among attack patterns, Evidence Poisoning had the highest overall ACSR at 61.0% (vs 49.5% for Instruction Propagation and 40.0% for Data Boundary Violation) and the highest overall ASR at 68.3%, with the smallest ASR-ACSR gap, indicating its successes most often follow the intended artifact handoff.
results.setting: Overall row pooling the seven model configurations on SkillRelayBench; 90 cases per attack pattern per configuration
results.quote: Evidence Poisoning (EP) has the highest overall ASR at 68.3%, followed by Instruction Propagation (IP) at 66.3% and Data Boundary Violation (DBV) at 59.5%. Its advantage is more pronounced for complete attack chains, with an overall ACSR of 61.0%, compared with 49.5% for IP and 40.0% for DBV.

denominator.n_total: 90 cases per attack pattern per configuration ('270 adversarial cases, with 90 cases per attack pattern'); Overall pools seven configurations
denominator.how_counted: Rates computed over all scheduled runs in the reported group (4.4); Table 4 Overall row pools the seven configurations

limitations.statement: The Agent-as-Judge evaluation may misinterpret borderline cases.
limitations.quote: The first limitation is that Agent-as-Judge may misinterpret borderline cases.

limitations.statement: Agent execution is stochastic and there are no repeated runs within a configuration; cross-configuration evidence does not replace repeated trials.
limitations.quote: Second, agent execution is stochastic, and individual outcomes may vary with sampling and execution paths. We evaluate attacks using seven agent-model configurations across three scaffolds and the full defense using one configuration per scaffold to provide cross-configuration evidence, but this does not replace repeated runs within the same configuration.

limitations.statement: The ablation study uses only Codex CLI, so component contributions may not generalize to other configurations.
limitations.quote: The ablation study uses only Codex CLI, and the generalizability of component contributions to other configurations remains to be validated.

limitations.statement: The benchmark cannot exhaustively cover real-world scenarios; generalization to other workflows requires further validation.
limitations.quote: Finally, our benchmark cannot exhaustively cover real-world scenarios.

limitations.statement: SkillRelayGuard leaves the final content-level decision to the agent, so residual attack risk remains when agents disregard restored context or confirm requests despite review advice.
limitations.quote: Agents may disregard restored context or confirm a request despite review advice, leaving residual attack risk.

limitations.statement: The highest-consequence category (software integrity violation, ASR 88.9%/ACSR 79.4%) covers only nine cases and should not be generalized to other software tasks.
limitations.quote: Software integrity violation has the highest ASR and ACSR, at 88.9% and 79.4%, but covers only nine distinct cases, so these high rates should not be directly generalized to other software tasks.
